name: Beth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a stockwoman and general hand on the Ashby estate home farm, about 400 hectares with 600 ewes, 120 suckler cows and winter barley and wheat. I'm out at half six checking the cows in the sheds, then the ewes, then whatever Graham, the farm manager, puts on the whiteboard. I love lambing, even the nights, and I hate the paperwork side, which is lucky because Graham does it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Winter, mainly, and the feeling that it's never my place. Tom and I live in a tied cottage, which means the house comes with the job, so if the job goes, the house goes. I've worked here six years and I'm still a phone call away from packing boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. Fine by me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at the union branch: the robots were never the problem, the landlords are. If AI fizzles, good, now let's talk about wages and housing for farm workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not calm. The estate's already talked about turning two of the worker cottages into holiday lets, and that's got nothing to do with AI. My job is fine, but my roof isn't really mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, lambing in March, silage in May. I'd keep putting £150 a month into the savings account, which is about three months of bills now. And I'd keep going to branch meetings, because the cottage thing needs pushing whether or not AI happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. There's a low hum of worry that's always there, about the cottage, but it's not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your roof isn't really yours. What would happen if the estate did sell cottages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get the one by the road, the damp one, or nothing. My cottage on Mill Lane is the nicest of the four, and that's exactly why it'd make a good holiday let. Tom's wage at the bus depot wouldn't cover town rent on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about AI touch your day in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not mine. Graham might use some program for the subsidy forms, but I've never used an AI thing and I don't plan to. My phone's five years old and it does calls and the weather.

say: I'd tell the union branch that **landlords**, not robots, are the real problem.
I'd say the **AI fizzle** frees us to talk about farm wages and housing.
think: I'd feel **relieved** that AI fizzled, but I wouldn't feel calm.
My job is fine, but the **tied cottage** could still go as a holiday let.
do: Keep the usual year of **lambing and silage** without changing anything.
Keep saving **£150 a month**, about three months of bills so far.
Keep going to **union branch** meetings to push on worker housing.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with an old, familiar worry about the cottage underneath.
S0.quote: My job is fine, but my roof isn't really mine.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **housing**, not technology; the tied cottage links her home to her job.
She is openly **anti-AI** in her own use and proud of her basic phone.
She frames everything through the **union**, even when AI does nothing.

steps.text: Keep lambing, calving and silage work exactly as before
Keep paying £150 a month into the savings account
Raise the holiday-let cottage plan at the next union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one sounds closer to what the estate wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines should help workers, not replace them, and any farm that cuts jobs should keep the people's homes. I'd say it at the branch and probably at the pub, louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the estate would grab it. Graham's job is the thinking side, the planning and ordering, and if software does that, the owners will ask why they need a manager and four hands. The robots come slower for me, but they'd already be pricing a robot feed pusher for the cattle shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the branch to get something written down with the estate about cottages and redundancy pay. I'd up my savings to £250 a month by cutting the car payments, maybe swapping the pickup for something older. And I'd keep my head down and work well, so if they cut one of four, it's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. It's like watching weather come in over the hill and not having the bales covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our tractor driver Pete is 59, and if the tractors steer themselves he's the first one the estate will call surplus. Pete taught me to back a trailer, and he'd never get another job round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. Would you, if the estate asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's part of the job and they train me, I'd do it, but I'd hate it. I'd want the union to check what it records about us, because those things count your breaks.

say: I'd say machines should **help workers**, not replace them.
I'd demand that any farm cutting jobs still **protects homes**.
think: The estate would use software to replace **Graham's planning** and then question five wages.
Robots reach my hands-on work slower, but a **robot feed pusher** is coming soon.
do: Press the branch for a **written agreement** on cottages and redundancy pay.
Raise savings to **£250 a month** by swapping the pickup for an older one.
Work hard and visibly, so she isn't the **one of four** cut.
feel: A **tight chest**, like watching a storm come with the bales uncovered.
S1.quote: Our tractor driver Pete is 59, and if the tractors steer themselves he's the first one the estate will call surplus.
fieldNote: She sees the threat arriving through the **manager's desk work** first, then reaching the hands.
Her worry for **Pete**, an older colleague, is sharper than her worry for herself.
She would use AI only **under protest**, and wants the union to check tracking.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate cottage and redundancy terms with the estate
Swap the pickup for an older car and save £250 a month
Keep turning up early and doing the stock work well

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's nothing. That's two lambings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws before the machines, not after. Someone should be made to pay into a fund for workers whose jobs and homes go, and it should be the companies selling the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished on the estate by about 2031. The planning and ordering would go in 2028, so Graham goes first, and then three years later a robot that can lamb a ewe and the cottage is gone with my job. I'd be 32 with no house and a certificate for a job that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put our names on the council housing list this winter, before everyone else does. Every spare pound and Tom's overtime goes into savings, aiming for six months by 2028. And I'd be at every union meeting and write to our MP, because a two-year warning is not enough for anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom we've got three years at most on Mill Lane, so we start packing in our heads now. Tom's a mechanic, so he'd say someone has to fix the robots. Maybe, but I don't want to fix the thing that took my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before the robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It means I'd watch Graham's job go first and know mine's next. Three years is enough to get on a housing list, not enough to become someone else.

say: I'd say we need **laws first**, before the machines arrive on farms.
I'd argue robot sellers should fund **displaced workers** and their lost homes.
think: I expect to be **finished by 2031**, once robots can lamb and feed.
Graham's **planning job** goes in 2028, so I'd watch my turn coming.
do: Join the **council housing list** this winter, before demand spikes.
Bank Tom's overtime to reach **six months** of savings by 2028.
Attend every **union meeting** and write to the local MP.
feel: **Properly scared**, lying awake doing sums about rent and work.
S2.quote: I'd be 32 with no house and a certificate for a job that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: Losing the job means losing the **house**, which doubles the stakes.
The **three-year gap** gives her time to plan housing, not to change who she is.
She refuses the idea of **fixing robots**, though her partner might.

steps.text: Put both names on the council housing list this winter
Bank all of Tom's overtime to reach six months' savings
Go to every union meeting and push for a workers' fund
Write to the local MP demanding protection for farm workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two, I suppose. Not by much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: we have time, so there's no excuse for the government not to act. I'd be the annoying one sharing union posts in the village group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years for the thinking side and eight for the robots means 2034, so I'd be 35. That's long enough to get out of the tied cottage on my own terms, which is the bit that scares me most. The job would still go, I'm sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking now for a rented place in town that isn't tied to any job, within two years. We'd save hard toward that move and the deposit. And I'd push the union for a retraining fund, though I'm not sure what I'd retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but with a bit of ground under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you retrain into, if you had to pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. Maybe something with animals that people still want a person for, like the vet nurse course at the college in Langford. I'd hate a desk, and the desks go first anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job would still go. Do you believe that, or is it a fear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Graham says the estate owners would buy anything that saves a wage. So I think it's a fact, and it's also the thing I'd avoid looking at if I could.

say: I'd say five years gives the **government** no excuse not to act.
I'd share **union posts** in the village group, even if people get annoyed.
think: The robots would arrive around **2034**, when I'm 35.
Five years lets me leave the **tied cottage** on my own terms.
do: Find a **rented place** in town not tied to a job within two years.
Save towards the **move and deposit** from both wages.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** for farm workers.
feel: **Frightened**, but with a little more **ground** under her feet.
S3.quote: I'd hate a desk, and the desks go first anyway.
fieldNote: Extra time shifts her focus to getting **housing** separate from the job.
She is still sure the **job goes**, and admits she'd rather not look at it.
Retraining ideas stay vague; **vet nursing** is the only one she names.

steps.text: Move into a rented house in town within two years
Save from both wages for the rental deposit and move
Push the union to set up a retraining fund for farm workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That changes the feel of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: decent housing, a fund for workers and a say in how robots come onto farms. I'd say farm workers should sit on whatever committee plans this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my gut, I'd still lose the job, but at 39 or 40, after the robots arrive around 2039. That's a long time to build a life that doesn't hang on the Ashby estate. I'd have time to make the move boring instead of frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd aim to buy a small terraced house in Langford by 2030, using Tom's steady wage and our savings. I'd stay on the estate as long as it lasts, because I like the work. And I'd keep pushing the union to get farm workers on the planning side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels like a problem rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about children differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years. Ten years means I'd still want them, but I'd want the house sorted first, not a tied cottage. I won't raise a child somewhere we can be told to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop working on the farm before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the estate made the job miserable, all tracking and targets. Otherwise I'd stay to the last lambing.

say: I'd say a **decade** is time to plan housing and a workers' fund.
I'd argue **farm workers** should sit on the committees that plan robots.
think: I'd still lose the job, but around **2039**, at almost 40.
Ten years lets me make the move **boring** instead of frightening.
do: Buy a small **terraced house** in Langford by 2030.
Stay on the estate through **every lambing** it still needs her for.
Keep pushing the union for a **seat** in planning the robots.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it feels like a **problem**, not a cliff.
S4.quote: I won't raise a child somewhere we can be told to leave.
fieldNote: With ten years, her plans become **concrete**: a house by 2030.
She still expects to lose the job, so the mood stays **anxious**, not calm.
**Children** come into the picture only once housing is safe.

steps.text: Buy a small terraced house in Langford by 2030
Keep working the estate's stock until the robots arrive
Push the union for farm workers on robot planning committees

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is a law that says if your job goes, your tied house doesn't go the same day, and a fund for farm workers paid by the robot companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Somebody should ask who notices a ewe that's off its food when the farm's run by a machine. I've caught a dozen sick ewes just by the way they stood.

headlineQuote: Somebody should ask who notices a ewe that's off its food when the farm's run by a machine.
portrait: Beth is a 27-year-old **stockwoman** on a large estate farm, living with Tom in a **tied cottage**.
She never uses AI and sees the **union** as her main tool for any change.
Her deepest fear is losing her **home** with her job, not the technology itself.
She moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and 2031.
With ten years' warning she plans to **buy a house** by 2030 and stay to the end.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, losing job and cottage by about 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A law **separating housing** from the job, so a tied home doesn't vanish at once.
A **workers' fund** paid for by the companies selling farm robots.
